title: No other gods
hook: first loyalty to the one God, before money, work or fame

segments.voice: Yesterday, the same commandments counted in different ways. Your line was ten words. Which one touched your day? Today, the first of them. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-four.

A bank statement, a calendar and a screen-time report. Lay them side by side and they tell a story: what got the first hour of the day, the first dollar of the paycheck, the first worry of the morning. The first commandment asks about the same thing in older words. "Thou shalt have no other gods before me." There may be no statue in the house. But money, work, fame and other people's approval all know how to ask for first place, and they ask politely. Today: no other gods.

The commandment doesn't open with a rule. It opens with a rescue. "I am the LORD thy God, which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage." First God says what God has done. Then comes the word: no other gods before me. Loyalty is an answer to a rescue. Some readers point out that before me can also be heard as before my face, in my presence: nothing else gets to stand in the room as if it were God. Jesus names one rival plainly. "No man can serve two masters... Ye cannot serve God and mammon." Mammon is wealth, money treated like a master. He doesn't say money is evil. He says it can't share the throne. You end up serving one and using the other. Martin Luther, explaining this commandment in his Large Catechism, turned it into a question: whatever your heart clings to and relies on, that is really your god. That makes the commandment a mirror. A rival god might be a career, a reputation, a child's success, a bank balance, your own competence. Good things, often. The trouble isn't that they matter. The trouble is when they get the first hour, the deepest trust and the final word. Luther also said this first commandment is the spring the others flow from. Put God first, the reading goes, and the other loyalties fall into their places, and they're loved better, not less.

Here's the practice: name your rival god. Settle, and breathe. Ask Luther's question slowly: what does my heart cling to? What do I check first in the morning, chew on last at night, trust to keep me safe? Let one honest answer surface. Don't argue with it. It may be a good thing. Just name it, plainly, once. Then notice how much it's been asked to carry. If you pray, you can hand it back to God in the quiet. The bell holds the time.
No other gods. The first word: loyalty to the one God who rescued, with nothing else allowed to take that first place.
Your line: first things first. Today, give the first five minutes of something, your morning, your lunch, your evening, to what you say comes first. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-four.

howItsDone: Christians learn this commandment in catechism, often with Luther's explanation in Lutheran churches, and some examine themselves against it before confession or communion by asking what they have put in God's place.

myth: the first commandment opens with a rule
it opens with a rescue: "which have brought thee out of the land of Egypt."
he says "ye cannot serve God and mammon": it can't share the throne.
for Luther, your god is whatever your heart clings to

fork.setup: you try to serve two masters at once, giving each exactly half. what does Jesus say happens?
options: you end up loving one and despising the other.
fork.reveal: "either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon."

original.note: Hebrew: other gods. The words of Exodus 20:3.

trapdoor: what you thought: no other gods means don't bow to statues of foreign gods.
what it means: nothing, not money, work or fame, gets the first place that belongs to God.
what a scholar hears: the command follows the rescue from Egypt, and before me can also be read as before my face.
recall: gathering in silence, waiting on God

notes: Teach quotes Matthew 6:24 with an ellipsis ('No man can serve two masters... Ye cannot serve God and mammon'); the fork reveal quotes the middle of the verse. Confirm KJV wording.

Luther's Large Catechism is paraphrased ('whatever your heart clings to and relies on, that is really your god'; the first commandment as the spring/source of the others). Confirm both paraphrases are fair.
'Before me' as 'before my face' (Hebrew 'al-panai') is attributed to 'some readers'; confirm.
'Mammon is wealth' — glossed without etymology. Confirm.
Original: אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים in Exodus 20:3; confirm pointing and pronunciation.

Editor pass: Luther's explanation now placed in the Large Catechism rather than described as written 'for ordinary households' (that fits the Small Catechism); added a source entry for the quoted 'No man can serve two masters'; practice's 'don't scold it' changed to avoid repeating day 1177's practice.
Audit pass (2026-10-02): Exodus 20:2-3 and Matthew 6:24 KJV checked; Luther's 'fountainhead' paraphrase is fair to the Large Catechism's conclusion; no changes.
